title: Using Libraries — Image Filters & Steganography
overview:
**Problem Set 5 — using the Pillow imaging library.** Part 1 converts an image to and from a flat list of pixels and applies a color-deficiency filter via matrix multiplication (uses `Pillow` + `numpy`). Part 2 is steganography: extract the low-order bits of each pixel to recover a hidden image.

What is auto-graded here: `extract_end_bits` (pure integer/bit math, no packages), plus `img_to_pix`, `pix_to_img`, and `filter` (Pillow-backed, checked against `image_15.png`). What is study-only: `reveal_bw_image` / `reveal_color_image`, which in OCW are graded by visually inspecting the recovered image against pickled staff fixtures — no crisp assertion, so read the reference and run them in the workspace. Source: MIT OCW 6.100L Fall 2022, Problem Set 5 (statements, provided `make_matrix`/`matrix_multiply` helpers, and image assets from OCW; reference solutions and tests written and validated for this study tool).

problems.title: Part 2 — extract_end_bits
problems.statement:
Implement `extract_end_bits(num_end_bits, pixel)`, the core of the steganography decoder. Extract the last `num_end_bits` bits of a value and return them as an integer.

- **BW pixel** (an `int`): return the integer value of its last `num_end_bits` bits. Example: `214` is `11010110`; its last 5 bits are `10110` = `22`, so `extract_end_bits(5, 214)` → `22`.
- **RGB pixel** (a `tuple` of three ints): apply the same extraction to each channel and return a tuple. Example: `extract_end_bits(3, (214, 17, 8))` → `(6, 1, 0)`.

The trick is just modulo: the last `k` bits of `n` are `n % (2**k)` — no string conversion needed. Detect the tuple case with `isinstance(pixel, tuple)`.

This one is pure arithmetic, so it auto-grades with no libraries.

problems.title: Part 1 — img_to_pix
problems.statement:
Implement `img_to_pix(filename)` using Pillow. Open the image and return a **flat list of its pixels** in row-major order.

- For an **RGB** image each pixel is a `(R, G, B)` tuple; for a **BW** image each pixel is an `int`. You don't have to detect the mode — `Image.open(...).getdata()` already yields the right kind of value.
- `list(Image.open(filename).getdata())` is the whole job.

The test image `image_15.png` is a 270×271 RGB image (73170 pixels). This part needs the `Pillow` package (loaded for you).

problems.title: Part 1 — pix_to_img
problems.statement:
Implement `pix_to_img(pixels_list, size, mode)`, the inverse of `img_to_pix`. Given a flat list of pixels, a `(width, height)` size, and a `mode` (`'RGB'` or `'L'`), build and return a Pillow `Image`.

- Create a blank image: `Image.new(mode, size)`.
- Fill it: `img.putdata(pixels_list)`.
- Return the image.

The test checks that a round-trip (`img_to_pix` then `pix_to_img`) reproduces the original pixels, that the size and mode are right, and that a small handmade pixel list is placed correctly. Uses `Pillow`.

problems.title: Part 1 — filter (color-deficiency simulation)
problems.statement:
Implement `filter(pixels_list, color)`. Simulate a color-vision deficiency by multiplying every RGB pixel by a 3×3 transformation matrix.

The provided helpers do the heavy lifting:
- `make_matrix(color)` returns the 3×3 matrix for `'red'`, `'green'`, `'blue'`, or `'none'` (`'none'` is the identity).
- `matrix_multiply(m1, m2)` multiplies matrices via numpy.

For each pixel: multiply the matrix by the pixel `[R, G, B]`, then **truncate each resulting channel to an `int`** and collect them into a `(R, G, B)` tuple. Return the list of transformed pixels in the same order.

- `filter([(214, 17, 8)], 'none')` → `[(214, 17, 8)]` (identity).
- `filter([(214, 17, 8)], 'red')` → `[(128, 126, 10)]`.

Uses `Pillow` and `numpy` (both loaded for you; numpy backs `matrix_multiply`).

tests.name: filters a whole list in order
black stays black under every filter

problems.title: Part 2 — reveal_bw_image (study-only)
problems.statement:
Recover a black-and-white image hidden in the least-significant bit of each pixel of `hidden1.bmp`.

Each pixel's hidden data is its **single LSB** (`extract_end_bits(1, pixel)`), which is `0` or `1`. Scale that up to a visible BW value (`0` → `0`, `1` → `255`) and rebuild the image with `pix_to_img`.

This is **study-only**: OCW grades it by comparing the recovered image to a pickled staff fixture (`tester_bw_img.obj`) and by eye — there's no clean literal to assert here. Read the reference solution and run it in the workspace against the bundled `hidden1.bmp` to see the hidden image appear.

problems.title: Part 2 — reveal_color_image (study-only)
problems.statement:
Recover a color image hidden in the 3 least-significant bits of each channel of `hidden2.bmp`.

For each RGB pixel, extract the low 3 bits of each channel (`extract_end_bits(3, pixel)` gives values `0..7`) and scale each channel up by ×32 so the recovered image spans the full `0..224` range and is visible. Rebuild with `pix_to_img(..., 'RGB')`.

This is **study-only** (OCW compares against `tester_rgb_img.obj` and by eye). Read the reference and run it against the bundled `hidden2.bmp` to see the hidden color image.
